subject: Maths
chapter: Chapter 3: Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables
central_question: How can two related linear conditions be modelled and solved, and how can we determine whether they have one, no, or infinitely many common solutions?
in_scope_units: Introduction: representing a real-life situation using two linear equations in two variables.
Graphical Method of Solution: intersecting, parallel and coincident lines; consistency; and coefficient-ratio conditions.
Algebraic Methods of Solving a Pair of Linear Equations: why exact algebraic methods are useful.
Substitution Method: expressing one variable in terms of the other and interpreting true or false identities.
Elimination Method: making one pair of coefficients equal and eliminating a variable.
Summary: consolidates graphical and algebraic solution types and consistency conditions.
banned_topics: Quadratic equations or nonlinear systems that cannot first be reduced to a pair of linear equations.
Matrix inversion, determinants or Cramer's rule, which are not part of the supplied chapter.
The cross-multiplication method, which is not developed in the supplied chapter text.

known_pitfalls.claim: Every pair of linear equations has exactly one solution.
known_pitfalls.correction: A pair can have one solution, no solution, or infinitely many solutions, depending on whether the lines intersect, are parallel, or coincide.

known_pitfalls.claim: If a₁/a₂ = b₁/b₂, the pair always has infinitely many solutions.
known_pitfalls.correction: Infinitely many solutions require a₁/a₂ = b₁/b₂ = c₁/c₂; if the first two ratios are equal but differ from c₁/c₂, the lines are parallel and there is no solution.

known_pitfalls.claim: A true statement such as 18 = 18 after substitution gives one numerical solution.
known_pitfalls.correction: A true identity with no variable indicates infinitely many solutions, not a unique solution.

known_pitfalls.claim: A false statement such as 0 = 9 means an algebra mistake must have occurred.
known_pitfalls.correction: When the algebra is correct, a false statement shows that the pair is inconsistent and has no common solution.

recommended_example_progression: Begin with the Akhila Giant Wheel and Hoopla situation from Section 3.1 to form and solve a pair of equations.
Use Table 3.1 and NCERT Example 1 to connect coefficient ratios, line positions and graphical solutions.
Use NCERT Example 4 to demonstrate the substitution method with a fractional solution.
Use NCERT Examples 6 and 7 to interpret a true identity and a false statement after substitution.
Use NCERT Example 8 and Example 10 to practise elimination and modelling applications.
ncert_end_of_chapter_exercises_reference: The supplied chapter contains Exercise 3.1 on graphs and consistency, Exercise 3.2 on substitution, and Exercise 3.3 on elimination and applications.
